title: The road of silk
text: The Silk Road was never a single road, and its name — coined by a German geographer in the nineteenth century — is a convenient {{1}} (SIMPLIFY). In reality it was a shifting web of tracks and caravan routes linking China to the Mediterranean, along which goods changed hands dozens of times and grew more {{2}} (VALUE) with every exchange. Few merchants covered more than a fraction of the distance. Rome worried about the trade's side-effects: senators complained that their wives' passion for Chinese silk was draining the empire of silver, an anxiety that sounds {{3}} (SURPRISE) modern. Ideas moved with the merchandise. Buddhism travelled from India into China along these routes, followed by other faiths, and — hidden among the cargo — the {{4}} (CATASTROPHE) arrival of the Black Death. Technologies moved west too: paper-making, gunpowder and the compass all crossed Asia, transforming Europe in ways no contemporary could have {{5}} (PREDICTION). Oasis cities such as Samarkand grew spectacularly {{6}} (WEALTH) on the passing traffic, and their rulers became renowned as {{7}} (PATRON) of art and scholarship. When sea routes proved cheaper, the whole system faded, its towns all but {{8}} (FORGET) beneath the sand until archaeologists began to dig.

gaps.explanation: 'the catastrophic arrival of the Black Death' — adjective from catastrophe.
'could have predicted' — the verb of this family is predict.
'renowned as patrons of art' — plural pinned by 'their rulers'.
'all but forgotten' — passive participle from forget.
